extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, students, and publishing professionals interested in genre fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and producing fiction that fits into established commercial genres (crime, fantasy, romance, science fiction, horror, etc.), including their defining elements, audience expectations, and market positioning. Useful for writers, editors, and marketers working in popular/category fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — intent to fit into a specific literary genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional works written with the intent of fitting into a specific literary genre in order to appeal to readers and fans already familiar with that genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term (also called formula fiction or commercial fiction) emphasises purposeful alignment with genre conventions and reader expectations; this marketing/intentionality distinguishes genre fiction from literary fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on plot and entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre fiction commonly implies that this type of fiction places more value on plot and entertainment than on character development, philosophical themes, or artistic depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of strong plotting and entertainment value is a characteristic criterion — works are often judged by how well they deliver genre-expected thrills, twists, or pacing rather than primarily by literary introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/category positioning (category fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In publishing the term 'category fiction' is often used as a synonym, with categories serving as familiar shelf headings within bookstores (e.g., Western or mystery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre placement and clear category labeling are important production/marketing criteria: books may be written or packaged to fit bookstore shelves and reader browsing habits; some literary authors publish genre work under pseudonyms to separate markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime fiction — subject matter and key elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime fiction fictionalises crimes, their detection, criminals, and their motives. Suspense and mystery are key elements to the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation/creation should emphasise credible criminal acts, plausible detection/investigation, motive exploration, and maintenance of suspense; multiple subgenres (whodunit, hard-boiled, courtroom drama, legal thrillers) have their own conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy — use of magic/supernatural and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy is a genre that uses magic or other supernatural elements as a main plot element, theme, or setting; many works take place in imaginary worlds where magic and magical creatures are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy is generally distinguished from science fiction and horror by expectations about scientific or macabre content; frequent conventions include medieval-style settings, invented cosmologies, and internally consistent magical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance — focus and required ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The romance novel primarily focuses on the relationship and romantic love between two people, and must have an 'emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romance works are evaluated on the centrality of the romantic relationship and the fulfillment of reader expectations for a satisfying emotional resolution; many subgenres (contemporary, historical, paranormal, erotic, etc.) modify but retain this core requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fiction — imaginative concepts and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction deals with imaginative concepts such as futuristic science and technology, space travel, time travel, parallel universes and extraterrestrial life; it often explores the potential consequences of scientific and other innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically SF usually eschews the supernatural and was intended to have at least a pretense of science-based fact or theory at the time the story was created; evaluation looks at idea-driven speculation, internal plausibility, and exploration of implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror — aim and affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror fiction aims to frighten or disgust its readers; although many horror novels feature supernatural phenomena or monsters, it is not a requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horror is assessed by its capacity to evoke fear/disgust and its handling of atmosphere, tension, and transgression; modern subgenres (cosmic horror, splatterpunk) trend toward less melodrama and greater explicitness and often blend with other genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-blurring / boundaries with literary fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works blur the boundaries between genre and literary fiction; critics' assumptions about artistic merit have been contested as serious study and hybrid works have grown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should recognise that literary merit and genre conventions are not mutually exclusive; hybrid works may be judged both by genre-fulfillment and by broader literary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-category segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most genres of fiction may also be segmented by the age of the intended reader: children's fiction, middle grade fiction, young adult fiction, new adult fiction, adult fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target age category is a production and evaluation criterion — tone, content, complexity, themes, and marketing must align with the intended age segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions and subgenre expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each major genre contains multiple subgenres (e.g., detective fiction, courtroom drama, paranormal romance, epic fantasy) with specific conventions and reader expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful genre fiction recognises and either satisfies or deliberately subverts subgenre conventions; creators and evaluators should be aware of typical tropes, pacing, and structural expectations for the chosen subgenre.
